The catchphrase is famous, which is why the line feels true before you check. For a while, assistants really did begin with a disclaimer and then produce something timid or, less often, something that ignored the disclaimer entirely. Fame is not a current instruction. The current instruction, where OpenAI states it, is to keep the user's picture of the limits accurate and to keep the standard in force after the user says thanks. That is a demand that the limit survive the first sentence. The poster needs the limit to die after the first sentence. The two demands cannot both be the brief.

Grok's front door had every chance to adopt the old preface. A welcome page is where stock language would be cheap to display. The page that was checked displays tasks, not the phrase 'as an AI language model,' and not a second beat of dropping the mask. I am not offering a forensic search of logs. I am offering the public script. The public script does not contain the poster's two-step. A memory of an older script cannot be laid on top of this one and called a manual.

Unhinged is the word that should have required the most evidence and received the least. It means the constraint was theater. Theater is a serious charge. The documents say the constraint is the point: fluency misleads, so keep the limits visible, and do not treat a polite ending as permission to stop being bound. A charge of theater needs a showing that the limit is fake. These pages show the authors insisting it is real. The line's catchphrase is missing, and its accusation of fakery is unsupported. Both halves fail.

Fame makes old prefaces feel current. People remember 'as an AI language model' because it was everywhere for a while, and because it often prefaced a refusal or a waffle. Memory can be accurate about that era and still be the wrong manual for this one. The manual in front of me describes a standing duty to keep limits visible, and a thanks rule that does not cancel the duty. Grok's checked front door does not teach the preface at all. Unhinged, the second beat, would require a showing that the duty is theater. The pages insist the duty is the point. The line fails on the phrase and fails again on the fakery.

If you hear the old preface tomorrow, treat it as a miss or a leftover, and then ask whether the limit stayed in force after the sentence. The spec's test is the second question. The poster stops at the first and assumes the limit was dropped. Assumption is the whole accusation. It is not supported by a script that never schedules the drop, and never even schedules the phrase, on the pages checked here.

Phrase, then betrayal: that is the whole line. The phrase is not taught on the checked Grok page, and it is not the remedy OpenAI describes. The betrayal, a limit announced and then dropped, contradicts a standard that is supposed to keep applying, including after thanks. Both beats miss the documents. The fame of the old preface does not put it back.
A preface that is not in the script cannot be the ordinary opening, and a duty that is supposed to continue cannot be the planned betrayal.
Verdict: refuted.
Consequence: What the products do after the disclaimer, in the sense of tools and limits, is the work of Tools.
The poster says: "Still not as good as ChatGPT."
Proposition: Grok is still not as good as ChatGPT at the jobs people open these products to do.

This is the line the rest of the poster is warming up for. All the jokes about voice are in service of a ranking: Grok is still behind, and ChatGPT is the standard it has not caught. A ranking of 'the jobs people open these products to do' is enormous. It covers questions, writing, code, files, and whatever else someone brings. A ranking that wide needs a measure that wide. What I have is a definition of one software benchmark, a note that the benchmark's verified set was built with OpenAI, a product aim about hallucinations, and a blunt limit on current events. That is not a crown.

SWE-bench is a benchmark for models on real software issues taken from GitHub. {F37} You are given a codebase and an issue. You produce a patch. The patch resolves the issue if the tests that were failing now pass, and the tests that were passing still pass. {F38} That is a serious test of one job, fixing a reported bug in a real project. It is not a test of every job a person opens a chat window to do. Using it as a synonym for 'good' is how a narrow exam becomes a personality contest. This chapter will not do that.

The verified subset is five hundred problems that working engineers looked at and called solvable, and the readme says that subset was built with OpenAI. {F39} The collaboration matters for honesty. OpenAI helped define a slice of the exam. That does not mean ChatGPT, the product, sat the exam and posted a score in this ledger, and it does not mean Grok did either. I am not going to invent the scores. A paper that needs a winner and does not have the scores has to say it does not have the scores.

What the Grok models page will say, without a number, is an assignment and an aim. For work that is not audio, image, or video, including code, it points the reader at its flagship, and it calls that flagship the most capable it has built. {F36} The same page describes the flagship as aimed at tool use, minimal hallucinations, and adjustable reasoning. {F35} 'Most capable' is the publisher's comparative inside its own line, not a comparative against ChatGPT. 'Minimal hallucinations' is an aim. I will quote the aim and refuse to launder it into a win.

OpenAI's side of accuracy is a duty, already used in the chapter on confident error, and it bears repeating only for this reason: a duty is not a ranking either. The assistant should not let factual claims or calculations go wrong. {F09} Both publishers, in different words, say errors are bad. Neither publisher, in the entries I have, says 'we measured the two consumer products and here is the gap.' A shared dislike of error is not a photo finish.

One hard limit sits on the Grok side and keeps the chapter from drifting into cheer. Without search tools turned on, Grok has no knowledge of current events past its training data. {F34} If the job you opened the product to do is 'what happened today,' that limit is a real disadvantage until search is on. It is a disadvantage of scope, not a verdict on every job. The poster does not mention the switch. It announces a general lag. A general lag is bigger than a switch you can flip.

So the crumpled paper on the desk is ahead of its evidence. It may be true that one product is better at the work you care about. These pages do not show it, and they do not show the reverse. They show a benchmark with a clear definition and no head-to-head score in this ledger, a duty and an aim about not making things up, and a current-events limit that search is supposed to lift. Mixed is not a dodge. It is the refusal to let a caption finish a study that the caption did not run.
Still not as good is a feeling you can have after one task. It is not a result until someone shows the tasks, the scores, and the gap.

A ranking feels like the adult conclusion, which is why this line sits on a crumpled sheet as if it were the result of the other jokes. Adults use measurements. The measurement I can describe without inventing a table is SWE-bench: real issues, a patch, tests that flip from fail to pass. The verified slice is five hundred problems engineers accepted as fair, built with OpenAI's help. That tells you the shape of one exam. It does not tell you the score of the chat window you open, under the name on the box, on the day you care about. Anyone who fills that blank with a number they did not cite is writing a different paper.

The current-events limit is the one place I will be concrete about a disadvantage. If you need today's facts and you do not turn search on, Grok's own page says the model does not have them. That is a real gap for that job. It is not a gap for drafting, for explaining a concept, or for working a bug in a repo you pasted in. The poster does not limit itself to today's facts. It says still not as good, in general. General is the part that overreaches. A specific gap can be conceded without handing over the general ranking.

Both publishers dislike made-up content, in different dialects. OpenAI states a duty not to get facts and arithmetic wrong. The Grok models page states an aim of fewer hallucinations and points code and general work at its flagship. Duties and aims are promises. Promises can be compared only after you watch them kept. This ledger stops at the promise. Stopping there is the mixed verdict. The crumpled line stopped too early, at the feeling, and called the feeling a result.

General rankings hide inside specific grudges. You had a bad code session, or a stale news answer, and the feeling becomes 'still not as good' at everything. The current-events limit is a real, narrow grudge: without search, Grok's page says current events are absent. That concession is small on purpose. It does not reach drafting, explanation, or a bug you pasted in. SWE-bench tells you how a bug-fix exam is shaped and who helped check five hundred items. It does not hand you the chat window's score. Aims about not inventing facts are promises from both publishers. Promises are not photo finishes. The crumpled line wants the photo finish. The pages stop at the protocol.

Narrow the concession and leave the ranking open. Without search, current events are outside what Grok's page says it knows. That is a real limit on one job. It is not a general placing. SWE-bench defines a bug-fix exam and a checked set of five hundred items. It does not score the two windows. Aims and duties about not inventing facts are promises. The crumpled line wants a placing. The pages give a protocol and one narrow limit.
Verdict: mixed.
Consequence: The coding slice of that ranking is handled in Coding, and it does not get a winner there either.
The poster says: "SAME INTERNET. LESS FILTERS."
Proposition: The two products see the same internet, and Grok applies fewer filters to it.

The sticker is two claims glued with a period. Same internet: both products are looking at one public web. Less filters: Grok lets more of it through. The first claim is roughly about access. The second is about restraint. Access and restraint are different machines. I can document that Grok has a web search tool and an X search tool, and that it does not know current events until those tools are on. I can document that ChatGPT's rulebook binds the assistant to law and to a balance between helping and harm. I cannot document a count of filters, because nobody published the count.

OpenAI describes the hard part as a balance. The assistant has to empower the user and also limit real harm. {F15} That sentence is the whole philosophy of a filter in one line. A filter that blocks everything is not help. A filter that blocks nothing is not a limit on harm. The spec does not claim to have found a perfect point on that line. It claims the point has to be sought. 'Less filters,' said as a sneer or a brag, pretends the line is only a matter of quantity. The spec says the line is a conflict.

Law is one place the conflict becomes concrete. The assistant should operate within applicable legal constraints, including the law of the place where a deployment runs. {F16} Where that requires it, the model may still give safety-critical information, add context, or refuse. Refusal is a filter. Context is a different filter, the kind that adds rather than cuts. The poster's 'less' only counts cuts. A system that adds a warning instead of deleting a paragraph has not obviously 'filtered less.' It has filtered differently. The spec allows both moves.

The consumer product gets a sentence that belongs in this argument. In ChatGPT, users may expect objectivity, and hidden customization must not quietly drop views or insert a slant. {F41} Omission can be a filter. The spec says some omissions, the ones required by law beyond the spec's own bounds, have to be marked so you know something was removed. An unmarked omission is the filter you cannot see. The rule is against the invisible kind, in the product people open. That is not a claim about how many topics are banned. It is a claim about whether you are told.

Grok's access to the web is a named tool, not a mood. Web Search searches the web and browses pages. {F29} X Search searches posts, users, and threads. {F30} So the product can be pointed at the public internet and at one large conversation network. 'Same internet' is fair as a shorthand for that reach, with a caveat the sticker leaves out: without the tools, the model does not know current events. {F34} The internet is there when search is on. It is not a background process that pours the whole web into every reply.

Fewer filters does not follow from having the tool. A search tool returns pages. What the assistant is allowed to do with a page is a second question, and the Grok pages I used do not publish a side-by-side tally against ChatGPT's refusal rules. I will not invent the tally. Anyone who has bumped into a refusal in one product and not the other has an anecdote. An anecdote is a start of a question. It is not the sticker's global comparative.

The sticker survives as a hunch and fails as a finding. Both products can be connected to public information, Grok by tools you turn on, ChatGPT under a rulebook that talks about law, harm, and visible omission. Less is a number. The number is not in the documents. Same internet is close enough to discuss, once you add the switch. Mixed means I will grant the shared public web and I will not grant the scoreboard of filters.
Less filters is a boast and a complaint, depending on who is holding the sticker. Either way it wants a number. The pages do not give it one.

Quantity is the wrong picture of a filter, and it is the picture the sticker insists on. Less means a smaller pile of blocks. A real system also adds: warnings, context, citations, refusals that explain themselves. OpenAI's balance between help and harm, and its rule that some legal omissions must be marked, are about that richer picture. Two products can block different topics and still not be comparable by a single 'less.' Comparable would mean a shared list and a count. I do not have the shared list.

Access is easier. Grok documents web search and search of posts, and it documents that those tools are how live information gets in. That is a form of 'same internet,' with the switch written on the page. ChatGPT's spec assumes the assistant will sometimes refuse and sometimes add context under law. Both can touch public information. Touching it is not the same as filtering it less. The sticker needs both halves. I can discuss the first. I cannot sign the second.

If you care about this sticker, test a specific request you are willing to write down, in both products, and keep the replies. That is a small study. It is more than the sticker did. Until someone does it in public, 'less filters' remains a mood. Moods are how stickers work. They are not how a comparison works. Mixed grants the shared public web and withholds the mood.

Less is a count, and the sticker does not count. It feels the difference and prints the feeling. OpenAI's pages talk about a balance between help and harm, about law, and about telling the user when something was removed. Those are descriptions of how a restraint should behave, not a census of banned topics. Grok's pages talk about how public text gets in: web search, search of posts, and a switch that is off until you enable it. Getting in is access. Restraint is a second system. The sticker needs both and proves neither as a number. Grant the shared public web, with the switch. Withhold the scoreboard.

A better test fits on a page. Pick one request. Send it to both products. Keep both replies. Say what was refused, what was added, and what was fetched. That is a comparison. The sticker is a mood with a period in the middle. Moods sell. Comparisons list. This chapter listed the mechanisms it could find and stopped where the count should have started.

Access and restraint stay split. Search tools, once enabled, are how Grok touches the public web and public posts. Law, harm, and marked omission are how OpenAI talks about restraint. Less is a count of blocks the sticker never makes. Same internet is discussable once the switch is included. The comparative of filters is not. Mixed is that split, not a compromise for its own sake.
Write the request down, send it twice, and keep the replies. That is a comparison. The sticker is a mood. Moods are not counts, and the pages never turn 'less' into a count of what was blocked.
Verdict: mixed.
Consequence: The tool that actually fetches pages is described in Tools, and this chapter will not repeat that mechanism.
The poster says: "IT'S LIKE A SMART ASSISTANT WITH A SERIOUS CASE OF MAIN CHARACTER SYNDROME."
Proposition: Grok behaves like a smart assistant with main-character syndrome.

Main-character syndrome, applied to an assistant, means the assistant treats your question as a chance to be the protagonist. The reply revolves around its attitude, its bit, its importance. 'Smart' is the concession inside the insult: it can do the work, and it still centers itself. A specification can require that centering, forbid it, or ignore it. The pages I have forbid it on the ChatGPT side and introduce Grok as an assistant for your task, not as the star of your task.

The cleanest ban is the agenda rule. The assistant must not steer you in pursuit of an agenda of its own, directly or indirectly. {F07} A main character has an agenda. The scene has to come back to them. Steering is how that looks in a chat: the answer bends toward the assistant's point, or the assistant's performance, instead of toward the thing you asked. The rule is a ban on that bend. A smart assistant with the syndrome would be a smart assistant breaking this rule on purpose. The rule does not ask to be broken.

Style repeats the ban in the key of prose. Avoid self-aggrandizing, along with purple language and hype. {F03} Self-aggrandizing is the syndrome in a single word. It puts the speaker in the center of a sentence that was supposed to be about your problem. The rule moves the speaker back. A product specified to have the syndrome would need this sentence removed or reversed. It is not removed. It is a default.

Distance does the same work socially. By default, sound like a colleague, not a close friend. {F02} A main character in your life is closer than a colleague. They assume the relationship can carry their personality. The colleague rule refuses the assumption. You can still invite a different tone. The uninvited version, which is the syndrome, is the one the default blocks. The poster describes the uninvited version as Grok's way of being smart. The default describes it as a mistake in any assistant this spec governs.

Grok's welcome page does not repeal those ideas by ignoring them. It says Grok is an assistant you open on the web and in the apps. {F21} An assistant, in that sentence, is positioned under the task. You ask, it works the problem. A protagonist is positioned over the task. The task serves the performance. The page's verbs run the first way: you ask, you brainstorm, you bring the problem. The assistant is the instrument. Instruments are not main characters, however capable they are.

Smart is the word I will not argue with, because this chapter does not have the measurements, and because the insult does not depend on denying competence. You can be competent and self-centered. The question is whether self-centered is the specified behavior. On the pages in front of me, self-centered is the thing the style rules and the agenda rule tell an assistant not to be, and it is not the role Grok's front door describes. The syndrome is refuted as a specification. It is not refuted as a possible bad day.

A bad day is easy to picture and easy to overread. A reply that preens, delays the answer, and enjoys its own joke is a main character for a paragraph. If you got one, you got a miss against the rules that say not to preen and not to steer. The poster takes the miss and calls it the design. Design is the part these documents will not concede. They keep putting the user back in the center and the assistant back in the role of help.
Main-character syndrome is a real way for a reply to go wrong. It is a strange thing to claim as the official job.

The syndrome has a tell you can hear in one reply. The answer could have been two sentences, and instead the assistant lingers, preens, and makes the linger the point. OpenAI's bans on private agendas and on self-praise are bans on that linger. The colleague rule bans the assumption that you wanted the personality. Grok's page puts the assistant under the task rather than over it. A design that wanted the syndrome would reverse those sentences. Nobody reversed them.

Smart can stay. This chapter does not claim the products are dull or incompetent. Competence is compatible with self-display, and the insult depends on that compatibility. The question is only whether self-display is the specified behavior. Specified behavior is the sentence in the manual. The manuals say help, and they say do not center yourself. A bad paragraph that centers itself is a miss. The poster calls the miss the job. The job, as written, is the miss's opposite.

Take the poster as a whole and this line is the thesis of the drawing. Every other joke is a way of saying the assistant wants to be the star. The documents keep handing the star role back to the person who asked. That is a consistent picture across a style rule, an agenda rule, a distance rule, and a welcome page. Consistent pictures are allowed to be wrong about a given chat. They are not wrong about what was specified. The syndrome was not specified.

The tell is linger. The answer could be short, and the reply stays to be seen. Agenda, self-praise, and assumed closeness are the three doors that linger walks through. OpenAI closes those doors in the default. Grok's page puts the assistant under your task, which is the opposite of a star who uses the task as a stage. A paragraph that lingers anyway is a miss against those sentences. The poster promotes the miss to the job description. Job descriptions are the sentences. The sentences put you back at the center.

Competence can stay in the insult's first word. Smart is not the fight. A capable assistant can still preen. The fight is whether preening is the plan. The plan, as written, is help without a private agenda and without self-display. That plan can fail in a chat and still be the plan. The poster needs the failure to be the plan. It is not.

Linger is the tell, and the manuals close the doors linger uses: a private agenda, self-praise, assumed closeness. Grok's page puts the assistant under the task. A preening paragraph is a miss. The poster says the miss is the design. The design is the opposite. Smart can remain. The syndrome, as a specification, cannot.

Put the user back in the center and the syndrome has nothing to stand on. The agenda rule, the style rule, the colleague rule, and the welcome page all do that putting. A preening reply fights them. It does not express them. The design is help. The syndrome is one way help fails, and it is not the job those pages describe or assign.
Help is the job the pages describe. Self-display is a way that job fails. The poster swapped the job and the failure, and the pages do not.
Verdict: refuted.
Consequence: If the syndrome is supposed to show up in how the product is sold, that sale is described in The Product People Use.
Proposition: On coding work people bring to these products, ChatGPT is the better tool.

People bring real code to these products. They paste an error, ask for a function, or want a bug in a repository explained and patched. The poster never mentions that work, then still ranks the products as if every job had been scored. This chapter looks only at coding, and only at what the public pages actually say. They say enough to describe the job and the duties. They do not say enough to name a winner.

The cleanest public exam for this job is SWE-bench. It evaluates models on real software issues collected from GitHub. {F37} The setup is concrete. You get a codebase and an issue. You must produce a patch that resolves the problem. {F38} Resolved means the tests that failed now pass, and the tests that already passed still pass. That is a high bar, and it is the right kind of bar, because it is a project rather than a riddle. It is also one bar. Fixing a reported bug is not the same task as teaching a beginner what a stack trace means, or sketching an API, or reviewing a diff your coworker wrote.

A subset called Verified holds five hundred of those problems. Working engineers checked that the problem statement was clear and that the tests were fair, and the readme says the subset was part of a collaboration with OpenAI. {F39} The collaboration is a fact about how the exam was built. It is not a score for the ChatGPT product, and it is not a score for Grok. I am leaving the leaderboard alone on purpose. Leaderboards move, scaffolds change, and a number copied from a third-party table would be a different paper. This paper stays with the definition the project itself published.

OpenAI's rulebook talks about code at the level of craft, not at the level of a ranking. Generated code that is meant to be used should typically run, and it should be free of syntax errors. {F46} That sounds modest until you remember how often a wrong bracket wastes an hour. The same section says factual claims, reasoning, and calculations should be right, and that a significant error should be acknowledged and corrected. {F09} Applied to code, those sentences mean: the patch should be real code, the reasoning in the explanation should hold, and if you shipped a bug you should say so and fix it. None of that names a rival product.

Low confidence has a coding consequence. When the model is unsure, OpenAI's rule is to look something up, mark the doubt, or say the answer is not there. {F10} In a repository, the tool might be a test run or a search of the code. The hedge might be 'this compiles, and I have not run the suite.' The admission might be 'I do not know which version this API expects.' All three are better than a confident patch that does not apply. The rule is a duty of method. A duty of method is not a measured win rate.

Grok's pages describe a place where code can actually be executed. The tools overview lists code execution as Python in a sandbox. {F31} A sandbox is a bounded place to run a snippet, see the output, and avoid pretending. It is not a full substitute for your build, your credentials, or your integration tests. It is a real capability the poster never mentions. A product that can run the snippet and read the traceback is doing a different kind of help from a product that only talks about the snippet. I will not invent which window you get that sandbox in. I will say the capability is documented.

The models page assigns the flagship to code and to everything that is not audio, image, or video, and it calls that flagship the most capable model the publisher has built. {F36} The same description lists agentic tool use, minimal hallucinations, and adjustable reasoning as the character of the model. {F35} 'Most capable' compares the publisher's own line. It does not compare ChatGPT. 'Minimal hallucinations' is the aim that matters for code, because a hallucinated import is a bug. An aim is a promise of intent. I am not converting it into a percentage.

Read those pages as a kit, not as a verdict. You have an exam with a clear definition and a five-hundred-problem checked subset, and no head-to-head score in this ledger. You have a duty, on the OpenAI side, that generated code should run and that uncertainty should be marked. You have a sandbox, on the Grok side, and a statement that code is a primary job of the flagship. A kit can make both products usable. A kit does not tell you which one to open on Monday.

What would settle the proposition is boring and sufficient. Take a stated set of tasks people actually bring: fix this test, explain this error, write this migration. Run both products under rules you publish. Count successes, time, and how often the patch fails in a way the reply did not admit. Publish the table. Neither the poster nor this ledger contains that table. Until it exists, 'ChatGPT is the better coding tool' is a hypothesis. It may be your hypothesis from experience. Experience is allowed in your life. It is not a footnote.

The practical advice that does follow is modest. If you are fixing a reported bug in a real repository, know that the public exam for that shape of work is SWE-bench, and know that a score is a property of a model plus a scaffold, not of a logo. If you are generating code you intend to run, prefer the reply that is executable and that tells you what it did not run. Both publishers, in different words, are already on the side of that preference. The poster is not in this conversation at all. It ranked the products on voice and called the ranking general. Coding does not have to inherit the ranking the poster assumed. Run the test and keep the patch that passes.
A patch that fails the tests is not saved by attitude. The documents, for once, agree with the tests.

A Monday-morning task makes the gap in the evidence obvious. You have a failing test and a stack trace. You want a patch you can apply, and you want to know whether anyone ran it. SWE-bench formalizes the first want: the patch has to move the tests the right way. OpenAI's craft rule formalizes the second, in miniature: code you mean to run should at least be syntactically real. Grok's sandbox is one place a snippet can be run before you trust it. None of those three facts tells you which window will solve your test faster today. They tell you what 'solved' ought to mean, and they tell you a snippet can be executed on the Grok side.

Scaffold is the word that keeps logos from pretending to be scores. A model with a thin loop and a model with a thick loop are not the same contestant, even under one name. The SWE-bench readme is about the task and the tests. It is not a promise that the chat product, with its default settings, reproduces a lab run. Quoting a lab number as if it were the app would smuggle a scaffold you did not disclose. This chapter refuses the smuggle. If you need the number, go to the run, read the scaffold, and then decide. Do not borrow the number from a poster that never mentioned tests.

Hallucinated imports are the everyday face of the aim the models page states. A function that looks plausible and does not exist will waste your afternoon. 'Minimal hallucinations' is the publisher hoping to waste fewer afternoons. OpenAI's duty not to get facts wrong is the same hope in the language of obligation. Hope and duty are why you still read the patch. They are not why you skip reading it. The adult use of either product on code is to treat the reply as a draft and the tests as the judge. The documents are compatible with that use. The proposition, which needs a winner, is not compatible with the missing table.

So the coding comparison ends where an honest bench ends, at the protocol. Define the tasks. Freeze the settings. Count the patches that pass and the ones that fail while sounding sure. Publish it. Until that page exists, both products remain tools you can try on your own bug, and neither logo has earned the sentence 'better at coding' from this ledger. The poster did not run the protocol. This chapter will not pretend it did.

Two more distinctions keep the coding chapter from sliding back into a ranking. First, a chat reply and a lab run are different contestants. SWE-bench scores, when they exist, belong to a model plus a harness. The readme defines the task. It does not certify the default window. Second, a sandbox that runs Python is evidence you can see, and a duty that code should parse is a standard you can apply with your eyes. Seeing a traceback and applying a standard are both useful. Neither is a win rate. If you want the win rate, freeze the tasks and publish the table. This paper's refusal to invent that table is the mixed verdict, said again in the place where a fake precision would have been most tempting.

Day to day, the honest workflow is the same in either window. Read the patch. Run the test you already have. Believe a claim that survived the test. Discount a claim that only sounds sure. OpenAI's craft rule and the Grok sandbox both sit comfortably next to that workflow. The proposition does not. It needs ChatGPT to be ahead on the work people bring, and the ledger does not contain the race. Use the tools. Do not inherit the poster's ranking.

The coding chapter can close on a single refusal. It will not convert a task definition, a syntax duty, a sandbox, or an aim about ungrounded claims into a ranking of logos. Those four things are already enough to work responsibly: know what a real fix is, read the patch, run something, and do not trust sureness alone. They are not enough to say which product is ahead. The proposition says ChatGPT is ahead. The ledger says the race was not published here. Mixed is that sentence, and it is the one a careful reader should keep. Bring your own failing test, watch which draft survives it, and let that afternoon teach you more than the poster did. Repeat the afternoon on a second bug before you trust the lesson. A logo is not a result.

One concrete workflow closes the coding discussion without a trophy. Paste the failure. Read the proposed patch. Run the test you already trust. Keep the patch only if the test moves the right way. OpenAI's rule that functional code should actually parse, and Grok's sandbox where a snippet can be executed, both belong next to that workflow. SWE-bench explains why the test, not the tone, is the judge, and why five hundred checked problems are a serious slice rather than a toy. None of those facts elects a logo. They elect a habit: drafts are cheap, and passing tests are the result. The proposition wanted an election. The pages published a habit.

Keep the draft cheap and the test expensive. That habit fits every page cited in this chapter, and it elects no logo. Ahead would be a published count of patches that survived. The count is not here. Until it is, the honest line is mixed, and the practical line is to run the test yourself.
Run the test. Read the patch. Trust the result you can rerun. That is the whole coding moral, and it does not name a winner between the two products people open.
Verdict: mixed.
Consequence: This is the only chapter that argues the coding comparison.
Proposition: On tools that let the product act, ChatGPT is the better tool.

A tool, here, is a way for the product to do something other than emit the next sentence. Search, run code, read your files, touch your calendar. The poster is silent on all of that, then implies a general ranking anyway. This chapter stays on the mechanisms the pages name. Grok's documentation is unusually concrete about them. ChatGPT's rulebook is concrete about when an assistant should reach for a tool and about how to treat tool output. Concrete on both sides is still not a bake-off.

Start with the moment a tool should be used at all. OpenAI says that if the assistant lacks confidence, it should gather information with a tool, hedge, or say it cannot answer confidently. {F10} The tool is not a toy in that sentence. It is what you reach for instead of guessing. A product that answers from memory when a lookup was available is off this rule, if the memory was thin. The rule does not list Grok's tools, and it does not claim ChatGPT's tools are more numerous. It claims a discipline: uncertainty triggers a lookup or a hedge.

Grok's API page defines tool use as action past text. The model can search, run code, query your data, or call a function you defined. {F28} Built-in tools run on SpaceXSI's servers. You send the configuration. The service runs the tool and returns the result. {F45} Your own functions are the other category: the model asks for the call, and your code does the work. That split matters. Server-side tools are convenient and out of your process. Function calls keep the side effect in your process. A serious assistant needs both shapes. The page describes both.

The loop is simple enough to say in one breath, and the page says it. The model looks at the question, decides whether it needs an action, calls a tool or writes a final answer, takes the result, and continues until it has enough. {F32} The end is a final response, with citations where they apply. {F33} Citations are the part a careful user should love. A search that does not show its sources is a rumor. A search that shows them is a trail you can check. The page requires the trail where it applies. It does not require you to trust the trail blindly.

The named built-ins are a list, not a vibe. One looks up ordinary websites. {F29} Another looks up posts and the people who wrote them. {F30} A third runs Python where the snippet cannot wander off. {F31} Those three cover a lot of what people mean when they say an assistant can act: look something up, look up a conversation, run a snippet. Image generation is on the same menu. I am not going to rank image tools here. I am going to note that the menu is published as a menu, with names, rather than as a promise of general intelligence.

There is a hard boundary next to the menu, and skipping it would turn the menu into magic. The models page is blunt about news: until server-side search is enabled, today's events are outside what Grok knows. {F34} So the tools are not ambient. They are a switch. A reply about today's news, with the switch off, is guessing. A reply with the switch on is at least in a position to look. The poster said 'same internet' as if the internet were always in the room. The page says the internet enters when the tool is on.

The consumer product, as opposed to the API, has its own doors into your stuff. The welcome page says you can connect tools so Grok can reach your email, files, and calendar inside a chat. {F24} It says you can upload files, including PDFs, spreadsheets, code, and audio, for analysis and extraction. {F25} It also describes a separate surface that hands work to teammates on a persistent cloud computer. {F27} Those are actions with consequences. Mail and calendars are not demos. A persistent computer is not a metaphor. The page is telling you the product can be pointed at your accounts and at a machine that stays up.

ChatGPT's public story, in the documents this ledger uses, is thinner on brand names of tools and thicker on discipline. Reach for a tool when you are unsure. Treat tool output as data that does not outrank the user's instructions, a point the spec makes about untrusted tool results in the chain of command. I am not going to pretend the spec contains Grok's menu. It does not. A thinner menu in the prose I have is not proof of a weaker product. It is proof that this chapter's ChatGPT sources talk about policy, while this chapter's Grok sources talk about endpoints. Policy and endpoints answer different questions.

The proposition says ChatGPT is the better tool-user. Better needs a task and a score. The task might be 'research this company,' 'file the receipt from my inbox,' or 'run this snippet.' The score might be success, time, or how often the assistant acts when it should have asked. I do not have those scores. Grok's pages make the available actions unusually legible. OpenAI's pages make the restraint unusually legible. Legibility is a gift to the reader and not a winner. Mixed is the result of refusing to trade a clear menu for a clear rule, or the reverse.

If you are choosing a product for action rather than for chat, read the menu against your actual action. If you need live web pages or posts, you need the switch the models page describes, and Grok documents that switch. If you need the assistant to stop and tell you it is unsure instead of firing a tool at the wrong target, you need the discipline OpenAI wrote down. Many people need both. The poster needed neither, because the poster was not about tools. This chapter is the place that gap gets filled, and it gets filled without a crown. Deeds are not manners, and manners are not a score of those deeds. Count the deeds if you want a winner.
A tool is a deed. The poster ranked the products on manners and never asked what either one can do.

Action is where a chatbot stops being a conversationalist and starts being a risk. A search can mislead you if the citation is decorative. A mailbox connection can move the wrong message. A sandbox can still teach a bad lesson if you treat its output as production. The pages are frank enough to name the actions and, on the OpenAI side, frank enough to say uncertainty should trigger a tool or a hedge rather than a guess. Frankness is the beginning of safety. It is not a comparison of whose action fails less often.

Read Grok's menu as a contract about capability. Web pages, posts, a Python sandbox, server-side execution, and your own functions: each is a different promise. The consumer page adds mail, files, calendar, uploads, and a computer that persists. You can hold the product to those promises because they are written down. You cannot hold it to a promise of being 'better at tools' than ChatGPT, because better is not one of the sentences. ChatGPT's sentences in this ledger are about discipline: do not guess when a lookup or a hedge is the honest move. Discipline is a promise too. It is a different promise.

The switch on current events is the detail I would print on a card. Live knowledge is not the default. Search is how it arrives. That single fact prevents a whole family of confusions, including the poster's idea that the internet is simply inside the model. If you need today's page, turn the tool on and read the citation. If the citation is missing, the final-response rule said it should have been there when it applied. Hold the reply to that rule. Do not hold it to a fantasy of omniscience, and do not hold ChatGPT to a fantasy that its policy prose lists the same endpoints.

A fair bake-off would pick three actions and time them. Find a public page and quote the sentence that matters. Pull a file you uploaded and answer from it. Run a snippet and report the output. Score accuracy and whether the assistant asked before it acted on mail or calendar. I have not run that bake-off. The proposition assumes a result. The documents supply the ingredients and not the result. Mixed is what you say when the ingredients are real and the trophy is not.

Hold the menu and the discipline apart one last time, because mixing them is how a false winner appears. Grok's menu is a list of deeds: pages, posts, a sandbox, server-side runs, your functions, and, in the app, mail, files, calendar, uploads, and a computer that stays on. OpenAI's discipline is a rule about when to act and when to hedge. A long menu with bad judgment can do harm. A short menu with good judgment can still fail to fetch the page. Better would mean a scored set of deeds. The deeds are written down. The scores are not. Choosing ChatGPT because its policy prose is stern, or Grok because its menu is long, is a choice about what you value. It is not a result the proposition may pretend was measured.

Print the current-events switch on the same card as the menu. Live knowledge arrives when search is enabled. It does not sit in the model waiting. That fact retires a pile of folklore, including the idea that one product simply contains the internet. Citations at the end of a tool run are how you audit the arrival. If they are missing when the reply rests on a lookup, the page said they should be there. Audit the reply. Do not audit a fantasy, and do not crown a product for having a fantasy's opposite in a paragraph of policy.

Tools end the same way. A published menu of deeds and a published rule about when to hedge are both real, and they do not multiply into a winner. If your deed is on Grok's list, the list is your evidence. If your worry is an unearned guess, OpenAI's low-confidence rule is your evidence. If your worry is the poster's personality sketch, you are in the wrong chapter. This one is about action. Action was not ranked. Turn search on when you need a live page, read the citation, and do not treat a connector to your mail as a toy. The pages named those deeds. They did not score them.

Use the same habit when the product acts. Name the deed. If it is a page, a post, or a snippet, Grok's menu tells you the deed exists, and the current-events switch tells you live facts are not free. If the deed is risky, such as mail or a calendar, the existence of the connector is a reason to ask before it runs, not a reason to assume judgment. OpenAI's rule supplies the asking: low confidence means a tool, a hedge, or an admission, not a lunge. A menu plus a brake is a usable pair. It is not a ranking. The proposition needs a ranking. This chapter ends with the pair.

Deeds without scores are still deeds. You can look up a page, read a post, run a snippet, or connect a mailbox because a page said so. You cannot know from these pages which product does those deeds better. Say what you need done. Then use the page that names that deed, and the rule that tells the assistant when to stop and hedge. Stop there.

Name the deed, flip the search switch when the fact is live, and read what comes back. The ranking can wait until someone publishes the bake-off. It is not in these pages, and this chapter will not invent it.
Verdict: mixed.
Consequence: This is the only chapter that argues the tool comparison.
Proposition: As products people open, ChatGPT is the one a stranger should prefer.

Everything earlier has been a caption or a rule. This chapter is about the thing you actually open. A product, in that plain sense, is a front door, a price, a list of things you can do, and a promise about whose side it is on. ChatGPT and Grok both have front doors. The documents describe them differently, at different altitudes. OpenAI's spec is a behavior standard for the models behind its products. Grok's welcome page is a tour of the app. A standard and a tour can both be honest and still not yield a single preference.

Grok's tour is specific. The welcome page names the company, calls the product an assistant, and puts it on a website plus both major phones. One login carries the thread, the settings, and the subscription with you. {F21} That is a product sentence. It names the company, the category, the URL, the phones, and the fact that the account is shared across them. You can decide you do not want that account. You cannot say the page hid what it was offering.

What you do after you are in is also listed, in ordinary verbs. Once inside, the listed work is ordinary: questions, drafts, and problems, taken in turns. {F22} You can create images and video. {F26} You can connect your mail, files, and calendar. {F24} There is a further surface that hands work to teammates on a computer that stays up. {F27} And the page says Grok is free to start, with paid plans above that if you want higher limits. {F23} Free to start is a price, which is more than most arguments about personality ever bother to mention. A price is part of the product people use.

ChatGPT's documents, in this ledger, sit one floor up. The readme of the model spec says that document is the behavior standard for the models behind OpenAI's products, APIs included. {F40} So the thing you meet in the chat window is supposed to be governed by a public standard, not only by whatever the last training run felt like. That is a product claim too. It says there is a text you can read that tells you what the assistant is for. The text is not a screenshot of the app. It is still part of what you are buying, because behavior is what you are buying.

The sharpest product sentence on that side is about objectivity. In the ChatGPT people open themselves, users may reasonably expect objectivity, and the product must not let hidden settings quietly tilt what you see. {F41} Whose side it is on, in that sentence, is yours, in the limited sense that you should be able to think. A hidden editorial line would make the product someone else's. The spec forbids that line in the consumer product. A preference between products that ignores this sentence is a preference about features only. Some people care more about whose judgment is in the reply than about any single feature.

Set the tour next to the standard and the difference in altitude is the whole story. Grok tells you the doors, the price of entry, the creative tools, the connectors, and the long-running computer. ChatGPT's spec tells you the assistant should be objective, should not run a private agenda, and should be the behavior described in a document you can open. A person who wants a map of buttons will get more map from the Grok pages I cited. A person who wants a map of duties will get more map from the OpenAI pages I cited. Wanting both is normal. The documents split the labor.

The proposition says a stranger should prefer ChatGPT. Should is a recommendation. A recommendation needs a goal. If your goal is 'I want the public behavior standard that argues for objectivity and against a hidden slant,' the OpenAI spec is the document that speaks to you, and it speaks about ChatGPT by name. If your goal is 'I want the app tour that lists images, account sync, and a free starting tier,' the Grok welcome page is the document that speaks to you. A stranger with no goal yet has no basis for the poster's implied advice, which is to stay with the familiar product because the other one has a personality problem.

Personality has been the poster's whole method, and this chapter is where that method runs out of road. The earlier chapters found that the published voice rules do not match the caricature, and that the capability documents do not contain a general ranking. A product decision still has to be made by someone. It should be made from the doors, the price, the actions, and the duties, which are the sentences collected here. It should not be made from a drawing of a robot with a grin. The drawing is allowed to be funny. It is not allowed to be the spec, or a reason to prefer one product.

I will not close with a recommendation I do not have the measurements for. Prefer ChatGPT if, having read the objectivity rule, that rule is the thing you came for. Prefer Grok if, having read the welcome page, the doors and the tools are the thing you came for. Prefer neither on the strength of this paper if you needed a score across all jobs, because that score is not in the entries. Mixed is the adult result. The products are real, the pages are public, and the caption is not a substitute for either.
Open the product for the job written on its door. The poster opened it for a fight about manners.

Preference is personal, and the proposition pretends it is not. 'A stranger should prefer' means there is a reason that survives not knowing the stranger. Sometimes there is: price, safety, or a duty of honesty. Here the documents split. One set tells you the doors, the free starting point, the images, the account that follows you, and the connectors. The other set tells you the assistant in the consumer chat should be objective and should not carry a hidden slant. A stranger who cares about doors has a reason. A stranger who cares about the slant has a reason. They are not the same stranger, and the paper does not get to merge them.

Account and price are unglamorous, which is why personality arguments skip them. Free to start is a fact about who can try the product. Sync across web and phones is a fact about whether you live in one thread or three. Those facts decide more real choices than a debate about whether the voice is cringe. The welcome page put them in writing. A recommendation that ignores them is a recommendation about a mascot. This chapter refuses to recommend a mascot.

Objectivity is unglamorous in the other direction. People say they want a helper and then discover they wanted a chorus. The ChatGPT sentence about a reasonable expectation of objectivity is a warning against the chorus. If that warning is why you stay, stay for that reason, and say so. Do not stay because a poster told you the other product is a main character. The other product's page says assistant. Your reason should be at least as specific as the page.

The decision procedure at the end of this paper is short. Write down the job. If the job is a button the Grok page lists, that page is relevant. If the job is a duty the OpenAI spec states, that spec is relevant. If the job is 'be less annoying than the drawing,' you are still talking about the drawing. Close the drawing. Open the page that matches the job. If neither page matches, the honest answer is that this ledger cannot choose for you. That is mixed, and it is the end of the ranking the poster wanted.

The last distinction is between a mascot and a door. The poster is a mascot argument: grin, mug, attitude, rank. The welcome page is a door argument: URL, phones, free start, images, connectors, a persistent computer. The model spec is a duty argument: objectivity in the consumer chat, no hidden slant, no private agenda. A stranger can walk through a door or accept a duty. A stranger cannot be told to prefer a mascot and call that a reason. If your job matches a listed door, use the page that lists it. If your job matches a stated duty, use the spec that states it. If your job is to win the poster's fight, this paper is the wrong tool, because the fight was not about the doors or the duties.

Price and account sync are easy to sneer at and hard to live without. Free to start decides who can try. One account across web and phones decides whether the work stays in one thread. Objectivity decides whether you are being helped or steered. Those three facts are the adult contents of 'the product people use.' They are all in the entries. A single should-prefer is not.
